title: Inflationary / Rising-Rates Regime: Macro Drivers, Asset Leadership, and What Fails
content: An inflationary rising-rates regime is driven by demand-pull or cost-push forces (fiscal expansion, wage-price spirals, supply-chain shocks, deglobalization) colliding with central-bank tightening, which pushes real yields higher and compresses risk-asset multiples. The dominant feature is positive stock-bond correlation: both asset classes sell off simultaneously, destroying the diversification thesis of classic 60/40 portfolios and producing their worst joint drawdowns in modern history (e.g., 2022, when the 60/40 lost ~16.7% on a calendar-year basis). Assets that lead in this regime are hard-money and real-return instruments: broad commodities historically beat equities in rising-inflation episodes (12 of 17 identified years), energy-linked structures (MLPs, royalties) track commodity strength, short-duration floating-rate credit reprices upward rather than down, and TIPS provide direct CPI linkage though with limited broader-portfolio hedge efficacy. Assets that lag or die include long-duration nominal bonds (price falls inversely with yield), high-multiple growth equities (whose long-dated cash flows are discounted at a higher rate), unprofitable credit dependent on cheap refinancing, and rate-sensitive sectors such as utilities and REITs that trade on yield-spread logic. Value equities, commodity producers, financials with variable-rate loan books, and trend-following CTA strategies tend to be relative outperformers within equities, while cash and short bills preserve optionality at the expense of real return.
lesson: In a rising-rates inflation regime the classic 60/40 bond hedge inverts into a second risk leg; survival requires rotating toward real assets, short duration, and commodity exposure while aggressively cutting long-duration nominal bonds and high-multiple growth equities before the tightening cycle peaks.
